column3: It repeats the focal act of taking desire as a god and adds its disabling consequence for hearing, heart, and sight.
It supplies the incapacity-to-harm-or-benefit test that exposes any rival to God as unfit for worship.
God's universal possession and sufficiency as wakil provide the true authority against which the messenger's limited role is understood.
Its question about rescuing one destined for the Fire parallels the focus's denial that the messenger can compel or guarantee another's outcome.
The preceding ayah identifies the mockery directed at the messenger in the immediate setting of the focal rebuke.
It explicitly forbids following desire because it leads away from God's path.
It joins exclusive deity with taking God alone as wakil, directly contrasting the focus's false inner ruler and limited messenger role.
It names worship of powerless things besides God, extending the focus's critique of misplaced divinity.
Its abyss uses a different sense of the root and does not address desire, worship, or guardianship.
Its rhetorical challenge about one who denies and turns away only broadly resembles the focus's challenge to a resistant person.
It forbids invoking what cannot benefit or harm besides God, a direct criterion against false objects of devotion.
The hearts being empty does not establish the focus's account of desire as a governing authority.
Its question about a person's guidance supplies only a broad rhetorical contrast to the focus's self-directed misguidance.
The immediately preceding ayah presents attachment to false gods and concludes with the same question of who is more astray.
It shows people taking gods besides God to obtain strength, making explicit the instrumental construction of false authority.
The prohibition of a worshipper is a nearby instance of resistance to guidance but does not itself explain desire as deity.
The next ayah explains the focal audience's condition as hearing and reason failing to restrain their straying.
It explicitly distinguishes the messenger's speech from desire, directly opposing desire as a source of authority.
The false claim that the Merciful has taken a child is another category error about divine identity, but it is indirect.
It challenges worship of things besides God that neither benefit nor harm, reinforcing the false-divinity critique.
The assertion that there is no deity but God is a general corrective to the focal person's private deification of desire.
It warns against attributing a child to God, a related but indirect distortion of divine identity.
Its command not to obey the deniers gives the messenger an active response without making him their coercive guardian.
Seeking honor through disbelieving allies illustrates assigning effective support and authority to a false source.
It explicitly denies that the messenger can compel people to believe, directly clarifying the focal question about being wakil over them.
The shadow's extension and the sun as its guide do not materially address the focal relationship.
The hypocrites' self-satisfied avoidance of hardship does not illuminate desire as deity or the messenger's guardianship.
It commands reliance on God and declares Him sufficient as wakil, directly supplying the rightful guardianship frame.
Following Satan and receiving punishment is a broad consequence pattern, not a direct account of self-deifying desire.
It contrasts following revealed law with following the desires of those without knowledge.
Its question about guiding the blind directly parallels the focus's limit on the messenger's power over unresponsive people.
It presents taking a path to the Lord as a voluntary response, consistent with the focus's refusal of coercive control.
It contrasts God's guidance with misguidance and says no guiding protector can be found for one God leaves astray.
The rhetorical address to one who denies judgment shares form but contributes only a broad moral setting.
The question to a people about what they worship directly opens the false-devotion theme.
Turning God's signs into mockery resembles the local rejection of the messenger but is not a direct neighbour relation.
Its question about making the deaf hear directly parallels the focus's denial that the messenger can control the audience's response.
Taking a close companion that leads one from remembrance shows a human relationship assuming a corrupt directing role.
Satan's claim to take an allotted share depicts exploitative claim over human allegiance, but it is indirect.
It asks who can plead before God or be wakil over people on the Day of Resurrection, sharply limiting human representation.
The people's declaration that they worship idols supplies a direct instance of devoted attachment to false objects.
It forbids following the desires of already misguided people and connects those desires to leading others astray.
Intercession is limited to one with a covenant from the Merciful, showing delegated religious authority is not self-claimed.
Those worshipped deny that they could take protectors besides God, directly rejecting a constructed network of rival authority.
God is made wakil over a human agreement, showing legitimate guardianship as accountable oversight rather than coercive possession.
It warns that following desire leads to ruin, directly stating the danger named in the focus.
The challenge whether idols hear their callers directly tests the authority claimed for worshipped objects.
God's supreme judgment does not materially develop desire as deity or the messenger's non-coercive role.
The question whether someone has taken a covenant with the Merciful challenges an unsupported claim to privileged authority.
The worshipped disavow their devotees, who then have no power to avert punishment or obtain help.
The command to fear God and not disgrace Lot has no focused relation to the focal themes.
The lost fish taking its way in the sea does not bear on worship, desire, or guardianship.
It explicitly exposes the calf's inability to answer, harm, or benefit, directly invalidating its claimed divinity.
God is named the deity of all people, supplying a concise corrective to any person making desire his deity.
The drinking of scalding water is unrelated to the focal claim.
The wrongdoer regrets not having taken a way with the messenger, directly contrasting responsive guidance with the focal resistance.
The declaration of one merciful God is a general correction to the focal act of assigning divinity elsewhere.
It asks whether the messenger can make the deaf hear or guide the blind, directly matching the non-coercion boundary.
The believers' prayer against Hellfire does not directly explain the focal error or role boundary.
It states that guidance and misguidance return to each person and explicitly says the messenger is not their wakil.
Jacob's sons' concern that he may perish does not illuminate the focal themes.
Abraham's rebuke of worship besides God directly calls the idolaters to reason about their false devotion.
Taking the calf after clear signs is another instance of wrongful worship, though it does not address desire as the deity.
The Torah's guidance commands Israel not to take any wakil besides God, directly defining the proper boundary of reliance.
The distribution of water and the people's ingratitude are not a focused neighbour to the focal claim.
The declaration that the deity is one directly rejects the plurality of authorities implied by making desire a god.
It identifies refusal of revealed guidance as following desire without guidance from God and calls it extreme misguidance.
It denies Satan coercive authority over God's servants and names the Lord sufficient as wakil.
Taking the calf during Moses's absence is a related example of false worship but remains less specific than the focus.
It instructs the messenger not to obey one whose heart neglects remembrance and follows desire.
The demand for the promised time does not explain false devotion or the messenger's guardianship.
The messenger declares that he is not wakil over people who reject the truth, directly repeating the focal limitation.
The description of the sky on the Day of Judgment has no direct relation to the focus.
The messenger denies independent power over harm and benefit, reinforcing the limits of his control over outcomes.
God's sole deity and certain gathering offer a broad theological corrective but no direct focal mechanism.
The demand for a garden and flowing rivers is unrelated to desire as deity or guardianship.
The question whether idols benefit or harm directly tests their fitness to receive devotion.
It asks whether they have a deity other than God and rejects their association of partners with Him.
It describes one who clings to the earth and follows desire despite receiving signs, directly showing desire displacing guidance.
It condemns worship of powerless things as intercessors besides God, a clear external analogue to false deification.
It warns against following other communities' desires after knowledge, a related but broader pressure on guidance.
Testing whether the queen recognizes her throne does not illuminate the focal themes.
A manufactured calf is explicitly called the people's god, displaying how a false deity is installed.
It shows people rejecting or killing messengers when they bring what their desires do not want.
The growth of a gourd tree for Jonah does not relate to the focal claim.
Building grand structures in hope of permanence does not directly address worship, desire, or guardianship.
The people command one another not to abandon their named gods, showing a socially maintained system of false devotion.
The debt-contract procedures do not materially develop the focal themes.
The idolaters admit that their objects do not speak, exposing the contradiction in treating them as divine authorities.
It warns against following others' desires after knowledge, but the setting is a narrower dispute over direction.
It reports shirk and then limits messengers to clear delivery, directly pairing false worship with the non-coercive prophetic role.
Their admission that God created the heavens and earth exposes the inconsistency of withholding full recognition and worship from Him.
The resurrection argument does not directly develop desire as deity or the messenger's guardianship.
Refusal to believe in God the Magnificent is a broad theological opposite, without the focus's mechanism of desire.
Moses's fearful departure and prayer for rescue do not illuminate the focal relationship.
It commands trust in the Ever-Living and sufficient Knower, supplying the true object of reliance immediately after the focal passage.
It forbids taking God's enemies as allies, illustrating an allegiance that wrongly gives opponents a directing support role.
Their arrogance when told there is no deity but God directly resists the exclusive divine authority required by the focus.
The modesty regulations do not materially address the focal themes.
It explicitly says the messenger was not sent as wakil over people, directly restating the focal role boundary.
It describes people taking equals besides God and loving them as God should be loved, the closest parallel to installing a rival object of ultimate allegiance.
It tells the messenger that their guidance is not upon him, directly limiting responsibility for another's response.
After distinguishing obedience and turning away, it says the messenger was not sent as wakil over those who turn away.
It confines the messenger's duty to clear delivery and assigns disclosure of what people reveal or conceal to God.
It explicitly says that the messenger is neither set as guardian over the idolaters nor made their wakil.
It warns that many mislead by their desires without knowledge, directly joining desire to unguided misdirection.
It forbids following the desires of those who deny God's signs and set up equals with their Lord.
It describes people with hearts, eyes, and ears that fail to understand, see, or hear, directly reinforcing 25:44's immediate explanation of 25:43.
It challenges associating with God things that create nothing and are themselves created, exposing their lack of divine authority.
It states that those associates can neither help their worshippers nor help themselves.
It says that calling such objects to guidance does not lead them, highlighting their incapacity to direct.
It calls all invoked beings besides God servants like their worshippers and challenges them to answer.
It catalogues the idols' inability to act, see, hear, or defend, directly testing the authority assigned to them.
The deniers demand a different Quran because they want revelation to conform to their desires rather than submit to it.
It separates guidance and misguidance as consequences for each person and says the messenger is not wakil over them.
Shuayb says he is not a guardian over his people, supplying the same non-coercive prophetic boundary.
Joseph contrasts many divided lords with the One Irresistible God, directly challenging rival authorities.
It rejects the names people and their forefathers invented as gods and locates judgment exclusively with God.
It says prayers to others besides God receive no answer, directly exposing the futility of delegated divine appeal.
It limits the messenger to delivery while God retains the reckoning, reinforcing the focus's separation of proclamation from control.
It condemns setting up rivals to God in order to lead others away from His path.
It says the beings invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created.
It states that the messenger's responsibility is only clear delivery when people turn away.
It forbids setting another god alongside God, which leads to blame and abandonment.
It repeats the prohibition on placing another god with God and ties it to condemnation in Hell.
It challenges those who call on beings besides God that have no power to remove or transfer harm.
It shows that even those invoked seek nearness to their Lord and fear His mercy and punishment.
It rebukes a people for taking gods besides God without clear authority for doing so.
It presents the truth from the Lord and leaves belief or disbelief as the hearer's own response, not the messenger's coercion.
It says the alleged gods will deny their worship and become opponents of their worshippers.
It argues that multiple gods in heaven and earth would have produced corruption, affirming undivided divine authority.
It challenges the taking of gods besides God by demanding proof for that claim.
It states that every messenger was sent with the declaration that there is no deity except God.
It asks whether the deniers' gods can defend them against God and denies that those gods can help even themselves.
It condemns calling on what neither harms nor benefits, defining it as far-reaching error.
It says the invoked object is more likely to harm than benefit and calls it an evil protector and companion.
It states that if truth followed their desires, the heavens, earth, and all within them would be corrupted.
It condemns invoking another god with God without proof and assigns the reckoning to God.
It describes people taking gods besides God that create nothing, are created, and control neither harm nor life or death.
It explicitly tells the messenger that he cannot guide whom he loves; God alone guides whom He wills.
It portrays those who take protectors besides God as relying on a house too frail to bear the role.
It challenges those invoked besides God as owning no atom's weight in heaven or earth and having no share or support there.
It says alleged partners own not even a membrane and have no share in God's dominion.
It says they cannot hear invocation, cannot answer even if they heard, and will deny the association on the Day of Resurrection.
It rejects taking gods besides the Merciful because their intercession cannot avert harm or save their worshipper.
It identifies the taking of gods besides God in the hope that those gods will provide help.
It rebukes the desire for fabricated gods besides God, directly naming false divinity as chosen falsehood.
It quotes those who take protectors besides God in order to draw near to Him, directly exposing mediated and misplaced allegiance.
It challenges the claimed power of things invoked besides God to remove harm or withhold mercy.
It says God is guardian over those who take protectors besides Him and explicitly tells the messenger that he is not wakil over them.
It commands the messenger to remain upright and not follow their desires, directly opposing desire with revealed direction.
It again limits the messenger's duty to delivery rather than control when people turn away.
It challenges those who invoke others besides God to show what their objects created or possess.
It calls those who invoke beings unable to answer until the Day of Resurrection the most astray.
It contrasts one who follows clear proof from God with one whose evil deeds are made attractive and who follows desires.
It describes hearers who leave the messenger without understanding because their hearts are sealed and they follow desires.
It forbids setting another god alongside God, a concise direct correction to rival divinity.
It says the deniers follow only conjecture and what their souls desire despite guidance having come from their Lord.
It identifies turning away from remembrance while desiring only worldly life as a distinct pattern of rejection.
It joins denial with following desires and refusal of a settled matter.
It commands that no one be invoked alongside God in places of worship.
It commends the one who restrains the self from desire, directly presenting the contrary response to the focus's self-deification.
It defines the messenger as a reminder, not as one who imposes belief.
It explicitly denies that the messenger is a controller over people, directly matching the non-coercive boundary in the focus.
It limits the messenger's task to delivery after people turn away from submission.
It identifies associating partners with God as a grave form of going far astray.
It rejects deifying the Messiah and affirms that God alone is the one to be worshipped.
It condemns the claim of multiple gods and declares that there is only one God.
It asks whether people should invoke besides God what cannot benefit or harm and be turned back from guidance.
It rebukes the making of jinn into partners of God despite His creating them.
It identifies God as the sole deity and creator, then commands worship of Him alone.
It commands following revelation that there is no deity but God and turning away from the associators.
It forbids associating with God anything for which He gave no authority.
It rejects worship of names invented by people and their forefathers without divine authority.
It repeats that the named objects of worship have no authority from God and awaits judgment on the claim.
It says those invoked besides God cannot help their worshippers or help themselves.
It describes taking religious authorities as lords besides God, a direct human analogue to installing a rival governing authority.
On the Day of Judgment the alleged partners disavow the worship directed to them.
It challenges the alleged partners to originate creation or restore it, assigning both acts to God alone.
It contrasts the God who guides to truth with alleged partners that cannot guide unless guided.
It says the gods invoked besides God did not help their worshippers when God's command came.
Abraham prays that he and his descendants be kept away from worshipping idols.
It recognizes idols as a source of widespread misguidance, consistent with false authority displacing guidance.
It forbids taking two gods and states that God is one, to whom reverence is due.
It condemns worship of beings besides God that possess no provision or power.
It depicts associators seeing their alleged partners and disavowing the association on the Day of Judgment.
It denies that God has a partner in dominion or a protector arising from weakness.
It rejects calling any god besides the Lord of heaven and earth as an outrageous claim.
It identifies God alone as the deity whose knowledge encompasses everything, correcting the calf's false divinity.
It denies that God has a child or any other god with Him, since rival gods would divide creation and contend for superiority.
It repeatedly contrasts God with the alleged associates, directing praise to God over their claims.
It asks whether any god is with God after naming His creative and sustaining acts.
It confronts the associators with the absence of the partners they claimed.
It says the alleged partners are summoned but do not answer, exposing their inability to respond or direct.
It affirms God's exclusive deity and judgment, a direct corrective to divided ultimate authority.
It repeats the challenge to produce the partners people claimed alongside God.
It commands worship of no other god with God and declares that all judgment belongs to Him.
It says idols cannot provide for their worshippers and commands seeking provision and worship from God alone.
It describes taking idols as a bond of worldly affection that will become mutual denial and curse in the Hereafter.
It says the associators will have no intercessors among the partners they assigned to God.
Its ownership parable exposes the incoherence of treating created dependents as partners with God.
It identifies associating partners with God as a tremendous wrong.
It recounts the angels' denial that people worshipped them, redirecting the claim toward the jinn.
The angels disavow the worshippers' allegiance and identify the jinn as the actual object of their devotion.
Abraham asks why people worship objects they carve with their own hands.
It rebukes calling on Baal while abandoning God, the best of creators.
It contrasts being called to deny God and associate an unknown rival with being called to the Mighty Forgiver.
It rebukes making equals with the Creator of the earth.
It challenges whether any prior messenger was sent with gods to be worshipped besides the Merciful.
It says the gods taken as means of nearness to God failed to help their worshippers and disappeared from them.
It states that the messenger calls only upon his Lord and associates no one with Him.
